title: Six things schools need to know about AI for the year ahead
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou of No More Marking sets out six findings about large language models for school leaders in the first September after ChatGPT. LLMs are already widely used by students, are excellent at fluent writing, yet make basic factual and mathematical errors and invent plausible falsehoods. She concludes that they are therefore poor at independent teaching, resource creation, or assessment, while being very good at passing written assessments. Her key argument is that an assessment matters for the inferences it supports about a student's thinking, and LLM-produced work destroys those inferences. AI detection tools, she adds, are unreliable and risk false accusations. The overall verdict is that LLMs are good at harmful things and bad at useful ones, so schools cannot simply ignore them.
points: LLMs are already in students' hands, even embedded in apps like Snapchat, so schools cannot assume non-use.
Fluent writing with unreliable accuracy limits LLMs as tutors, resource creators and assessors.
Out-of-class written assessment is threatened because the point of assessment is the inference about a student's thinking, which LLM work destroys.
AI detectors are unreliable and misclassify human writing, leading to corrosive false accusations.
LLMs are good at harmful things like cheating and bad at useful things like instruction, so schools must respond.
quotes: They can write really well. They barely make any technical errors, and they are excellent at mimicking the tone or style of particular writers or genres.

Yes, they will repeat the kinds of misconceptions and misinformation that are out there already on the internet. But in addition to this, they will make basic maths errors, and they invent completely new and plausible "facts" that are totally incorrect.

This is more controversial - but I think the error rate and error type of LLMs limits their educational applications. I don’t think they can be used as independent personal tutors, because the potential for confusion and misunderstanding is huge.

Briefly: the point of an assessment is not the quality of the final product, but the inferences you can make about a student's thinking based on that final product. Work completed by LLMs destroys those inferences.

A lot of tools claim this is possible, but most of the emerging data shows they don't work reliably. Not only that, but as well as failing to identify AI writing, they also misclassify real human writing as AI. In practice, this means false accusations of cheating, which are incredibly serious and enormously corrosive to classroom relationships.

Being good at language and bad at accuracy is a toxic combination. It basically means that LLMs are really good at educationally & socially harmful things like cheating, but really bad at educationally & socially useful things like aiding instruction, assessing accurately, etc.
